pairs.rationale: Both accounts address Theophilus and describe the writing of a narrative. Acts recalls its first account about Jesus' deeds and teaching; Luke explains its orderly account and purpose of assurance. The shared addressee is not given an additional unrecorded biography.

Both describe Jesus being taken into heaven after His ministry with the disciples. Acts adds Spirit-mediated instructions to chosen apostles; Luke describes the Bethany setting and blessing. Luke does not repeat every detail of the Spirit's role stated in Acts.

Luke describes a post-suffering appearance with bodily evidence and eating; Acts summarizes many proofs and appearances over forty days. This supplies a concrete resurrection-appearance comparison without making Luke's single scene the entirety of Acts' forty-day period.

Both have Jesus tell His followers to remain in the city for the Father's promise. Luke describes clothing with power from on high; Acts explicitly says not to leave Jerusalem while awaiting that promise. The different power images are retained.

Jesus recalls the contrast between John's water baptism and the coming baptism in the Holy Spirit. Luke records John's water/Spirit contrast and additionally mentions fire. Acts' timing promise does not itself add fire to this sentence.

Both use restoration and time language concerning Jesus' mission. Here followers ask about restoring Israel's kingdom; Peter later speaks of refreshing and the restoration of all things announced by prophets. The later speech does not supply the date withheld in the following answer.

Both reserve timing knowledge to the Father. Matthew concerns the day and hour and names others who do not know; Acts concerns times and seasons set by the Father's authority. The questions and temporal terms differ rather than providing a restoration calendar.

Both join Jerusalem-starting witness with promised power. Luke speaks of all nations and being clothed with power from on high; Acts specifies the Spirit, Judea, Samaria, and the earth's end. Their geographical and image formulations remain distinct.

Both narrate Jesus' ascension in the followers' presence. Luke adds His blessing and the Bethany setting; Acts adds their watching and the cloud taking Him from sight. The cloud is not silently inserted into Luke's wording.

Both describe two male figures standing beside witnesses in distinctive garments. Luke places flashing clothing at the empty tomb; Acts places white garments during the ascension. The recurring scene pattern does not identify them as the same two individuals.

The promised return of the ascended Jesus can be compared with the Son of Man's coming on heaven's clouds. Acts' preceding cloud belongs to His departure; Matthew adds power, glory, and mourning. The comparison does not fix the date or collapse departure and return into one event.

Both describe the followers' return to Jerusalem after the ascension. Acts gives Olivet and the Sabbath-journey distance; Luke gives worship and great joy. The distance description and the response of joy are different retained details.

The eleven named here correspond to members of Luke's earlier Twelve list, while Judas Iscariot is absent. Luke narrates their initial selection and includes the betrayer; Acts records the remaining group before replacement. The comparison traces named membership across their initial selection and the later vacancy.

John earlier states that Jesus' brothers did not believe in Him; Acts later places His brothers in common prayer with His mother and the apostles. The reports differ in setting, and neither supplies an exact date or individual account of each brother's change.

Both present Peter rising to address fellow believers during a communal decision. Acts 1 concerns the apostolic vacancy in the following speech; Acts 15 concerns the Gentile question. The recurring speaker pattern does not equate the meetings or their decisions.

Peter identifies Judas as a guide to Jesus' arresters; Luke describes Judas, one of the Twelve, going ahead of the crowd toward Jesus. Acts also interprets Scripture's fulfillment, which is not itself stated in Luke's arrest-introduction verse.

Both place Judas within the chosen Twelve before his betrayal. Acts emphasizes his counted membership and ministry share; John records Jesus choosing the Twelve and identifies the prospective betrayer. The chosen status is not mistaken for an endorsement of the betrayal.

Both associate Judas, betrayal payment, death, and a field. Acts describes his acquiring a field and falling headlong with his body bursting; Matthew describes returned money, hanging, and a priestly purchase. No unrecorded rope-breaking or combined sequence is supplied.

Both explain a field called Blood in connection with Judas' payment. Acts supplies the local name Hakeldamach and public knowledge; Matthew gives the priests' blood-money discussion and purchase. Their stated details and purchase agencies are not made identical.

Peter applies the deserted-dwelling Psalm language to Judas. The Psalm speaks of their homestead and dwellings; Acts gives the application in the singular. The original Psalm does not name Judas, and its plural wording is not silently rewritten.

Peter quotes the request that another receive the office of oversight. The Psalm joins that request with shortened days; Acts applies it to the apostolic vacancy. The quoted office language does not itself describe Matthias' later selection procedure.

Acts seeks a replacement from those who accompanied Jesus; Mark describes the initial Twelve being appointed to be with Him and be sent. The shared companionship-and-ministry pattern does not say the two candidates were in Mark's original Twelve.

Both assign witness concerning Jesus' resurrection and mission to His followers. Acts defines the replacement candidate's accompanying period from John's baptism through ascension; Luke sets witness after the suffering-and-resurrection declaration. The candidate criteria are not made a universal rule for every later ministry.

Both appeal to divine knowledge of hearts in a community decision. Acts 1 asks the Lord to show the chosen candidate; Acts 15 describes God knowing hearts and giving the Spirit to Gentiles without distinction. The different decisions and divine titles remain as written.

Acts describes Judas leaving his apostolic ministry; Jesus' prayer describes the loss exception as the son of destruction and relates it to Scripture. This is a contextual comparison concerning the betrayer, not a supplied geographical definition of 'his own place.'

Both use lots in a religiously framed decision. Acts reports Matthias selected after prayer for the Lord's choice; Joshua casts lots before the Lord for land division. The procedure's different purpose is retained rather than making land allocation an apostolic succession rule.

Leviticus counts seven weeks and fifty days before the new grain offering. This supplies festival-calendar background for Pentecost in Acts; it does not narrate the Spirit's arrival or determine the number of people gathered in the house.

Both join wind or its sound with Spirit language. Acts describes a sound like a rushing violent wind; Jesus' saying uses the wind's sound and movement to describe those born of the Spirit. The images are compared without turning Acts' likeness into a stated physical storm.

Luke joins Holy Spirit and fire in John's baptism announcement; Acts describes distributed tongues like fire at the Spirit's arrival. This is a qualified image comparison, not an assertion that Acts exhausts every meaning of fire in John's announcement.

The Spirit's arrival realizes the core of Jesus' near-term promise. Acts 2 describes filling and Spirit-given speech in other tongues; Acts 1 uses baptism language and does not specify the languages. The different descriptions are retained.

Deuteronomy requires festival appearance before the Lord, including the Feast of Weeks. Acts describes devout Jews from many nations living in Jerusalem. The festival law is background, not proof that every person described was only a temporary pilgrim.

Genesis describes language confusion that prevents mutual understanding and scatters people; Acts describes bewilderment because each hears his own language. This is a contrasting language-and-gathering comparison, not an assertion that Pentecost made every language one language again.

Acts' hearers question the Galilean identity of the speakers; Luke's accuser identifies Peter as a Galilean during the denial. These are different reported reactions. Neither supplies a complete account of the languages normally spoken by all Galileans.

The native-language question corresponds to the narrator's earlier description of Spirit-given speech and each hearer's own-language hearing. This links the crowd's perplexity with the narrated phenomenon; no separately named interpreter or second language miracle is added.

The hearers say they hear God's mighty deeds in their languages; the Psalm calls for His wonders to be declared among all peoples. The content and international scope correspond, without claiming the Psalm names these particular languages or predicts Pentecost explicitly.

The crowd asks what the phenomenon means; Peter subsequently identifies it through Joel's Spirit-outpouring prophecy. This is the question-and-explanation development within one account, not an independent second witness or a claim that the whole crowd accepted the explanation.

Both describe an adverse outsider reaction to tongues. Acts reports a charge of sweet-wine drunkenness; Paul describes outsiders potentially calling an assembled tongue-speaking church mad. The reactions and settings differ, and neither accusation is endorsed.

Peter stands with the eleven after Matthias has been counted with the eleven apostles. The preceding replacement supplies the membership context for the public apostolic group. This is an internal narrative connection, not another list of individually named participants.

Peter denies drunkenness before explaining the Spirit's work; Ephesians contrasts drunkenness with being filled with the Spirit. Acts also gives the third-hour observation. The negative statement is preserved rather than treating drunkenness as the prescribed spiritual condition.

Peter explicitly identifies Joel as the prophetic source of the following citation. The saved Joel division places this passage in chapter3. Acts applies its outpouring language here without separately narrating every cosmic sign in the quoted passage as already completed.

Both describe God's Spirit poured upon all flesh and sons, daughters, elders, and young men receiving prophetic revelations. Acts introduces last-days wording and places young men before elders; Joel's temporal introduction and order are retained as written.

Both extend the Spirit's outpouring to male and female slaves. Acts explicitly adds that they will prophesy. The servant status and both sexes are retained without replacing the original terms with a different social category.

Both announce heavenly and earthly wonders with blood, fire, and smoke imagery. Acts adds above/below distinctions and the word signs in its presentation. The quotation comparison does not claim these physical signs are all narrated as occurring in the house.

Both describe the sun's darkening and the moon becoming blood before the Lord's great day. The comparison follows the saved Greek-based division rather than substituting another edition's chapter numbering or supplying a modern date.

Acts quotes the promise that everyone invoking the Lord's name will be saved. Joel continues with Zion, Jerusalem, and the Lord's calling. Acts' quoted clause is not treated as if it reproduced the entirety of Joel's verse.

Peter describes God's works through Jesus as attestation; Jesus in John describes the Father's given works as testimony that He was sent. The speakers and settings differ, while the works-and-divine-witness relation is shared.

Both hold divine purpose and human responsibility together. Acts names God's determined purpose and foreknowledge alongside its addressed hearers' killing through lawless hands; Luke says the Son of Man goes as determined and pronounces woe on the betrayer. The particular agents differ.

Both connect Jesus' resurrection with death's inability to retain dominion. Acts speaks of God releasing death's pangs and its inability to hold Him; Romans says the risen Christ no longer dies and death no longer rules Him. Their explanatory images differ.

Peter introduces David's words about keeping the Lord before him and being unshaken with the Lord at his right hand. The Psalm supplies that first-person statement; Peter's Christ-directed application is the speech's interpretation.

Both describe the rejoicing heart and tongue and flesh dwelling in hope. The Psalm's bodily hope language is retained; Peter's surrounding argument interprets it in relation to Jesus' resurrection rather than making David's body undying in its tomb.

The citation joins the soul not being abandoned to Hades with the Holy One not seeing decay. The Psalm supplies the wording, while Peter's following argument identifies its resurrection application. Hades is not silently replaced with a different afterlife term.

Both speak of made-known paths of life and joy in God's presence. The Psalm continues beyond the portion quoted in Acts. The comparison preserves the quotation's actual extent rather than adding every remaining Psalm phrase to Peter's words.

Kings narrates David's death and burial in the city of David, the ancestral fact Peter invokes. Acts additionally asserts the tomb's continuing presence among its hearers. The older narrative does not identify a modern tomb location.

Peter recalls God's oath to David concerning a descendant upon his throne. The Psalm supplies the sworn throne-and-offspring promise. The offspring expressions in the two passages are compared as written rather than silently making their complete sentences identical.

Peter explicitly interprets the Hades-and-decay saying as foreseen speech about the Christ's resurrection. The Psalm itself does not name Jesus, and Acts' explanatory flesh-language is distinguished from the Psalm's designation of the Holy One.

Jesus' resurrection-and-witness instruction in Luke is followed by Peter's declaration that God raised Jesus and the group are witnesses. This links commission with subsequent testimony within the literary sequence rather than claiming the accounts are independent historical attestations.

John anticipates believers receiving the Spirit in relation to Jesus' glorification; Acts describes the exalted Jesus receiving the Father's promised Spirit and pouring out what is seen and heard. The giver/receiver roles and John's exact 'Spirit was not yet' wording remain distinct.

Peter introduces the Lord's address to 'my Lord' and the right-hand command. The Psalm contains the whole instruction, which Acts divides across two source units. Peter's statement about David not ascending is part of his interpretation, not a verbatim line in this Psalm.

This continues the cited command with enemies made a footstool. The same Psalm verse also contains the preceding right-hand clause. Preserving the whole target verse keeps the divided Acts quotation in its original scriptural context.

Both associate divine exaltation with Jesus' lordship. Acts calls the crucified Jesus Lord and Christ; Philippians describes God's exaltation and confession of Jesus Christ as Lord to the Father's glory. The made-Lord and exaltation formulations remain distinct.

Both crowds ask what they should do in response to proclamation. Acts describes pierced hearts and Peter's subsequent repentance-and-baptism answer; Luke has John's instruction about sharing clothing and food. The same question is not given an identical answer in both scenes.

Peter's call to repentance and forgiveness in Jesus Christ's name develops Jesus' Jerusalem-starting proclamation commission and promised power. Acts additionally names baptism and the Spirit's gift. Luke's commission is not rewritten as the exact baptism formula spoken here.

Peter extends the promise to hearers, their children, and those far away whom God calls; Joel's ending names bearers of good news whom the Lord called. The calling language corresponds, while the descriptions of recipients and messengers are not declared identical.

Peter's crooked-generation warning recalls the crooked-generation language of Moses' song. Acts calls the present hearers to be saved; Deuteronomy censures unfaithful conduct. This is a moral and verbal comparison, not an inherited judgment upon every later descendant.

Both describe growth following reception of the word. Acts 2 reports about three thousand persons baptized and added that day; Acts 4 gives a total of about five thousand men. The figures have different descriptions and are not treated as two identical new additions.

Both community gatherings combine instruction with breaking bread. Acts 2 also lists fellowship and prayers; Acts 20 describes a first-day gathering and Paul's extended speech. The comparison does not decide every meal's ritual status beyond the supplied wording.

Both summarize many signs and wonders through the apostles. Acts 2 adds general awe; Acts 5 specifies the apostles' hands and the united gathering at Solomon's Portico. These are internal recurring summaries, not independent records of each individual sign.

Both describe believers sharing possessions in common. Acts 4 expands the description with one heart and soul and no private ownership claim within the sharing practice. This is the narrative's expanded community description, not independent attestation or an added legal ownership statute.

Jesus tells His followers to sell possessions and give alms; Acts describes repeated sales and distribution according to need. Luke adds heavenly-treasure imagery, while Acts describes the community's practice. The command and the later descriptive action retain their different forms.

Both describe daily activity in the Temple and in homes. Acts 2 emphasizes shared food, gladness, and simplicity of heart; Acts 5 emphasizes teaching and proclaiming Jesus as Christ. The shared locations do not make their complete activity lists identical.

Both join public regard for the believers with growth. Acts 2 includes praise and daily additions by the Lord; Acts 5 includes high esteem, reluctance to join, and added men and women. Its stated reluctance is not erased by treating public approval as universal membership.

Peter and John go to Temple prayer at the ninth hour; Cornelius later describes praying at home at the ninth hour. The shared prayer hour does not identify the places, participants, or subsequent events as the same.

Both describe a man unable to walk from his mother's womb. Acts 14 explicitly adds never having walked and locates the man at Lystra; Acts 3 places its man at the Beautiful Gate for alms. These are distinct congenital-disability healings.

Both apostolic healing scenes describe an intent look at the disabled man. Acts 3 also records the command to look at Peter and John; Acts 14 says Paul perceived faith for healing. Paul's explicit perception is not silently assigned to the earlier scene.

Peter commands 'get up and walk' in Jesus Christ's name; Luke has Jesus tell the paralyzed man to rise, take his bed, and go home. The commands and recovery correspond, while the actors, conditions, and bed detail differ.

Both healing scenes include taking the person's hand and raising the person. Peter takes a right hand and the man's feet and ankles become strong; Jesus raises the fevered woman and her fever leaves. The people and illnesses are different.

The healed man's leaping can be compared with Isaiah's promise of a lame person leaping like a deer. Acts adds walking into the Temple and praising God. This is a possible restoration-image echo, not a direct quotation or an assertion that every other Isaiah image occurs here.

Both describe public observation of a healed person praising God. Luke's formerly blind man follows Jesus and the onlookers also praise God; Acts' man walks and praises while the people see him. Their disabilities and the precise observers' responses differ.

Both connect public response with recognizing a formerly disabled beggar. Acts' people recognize the Temple beggar and marvel; John's neighbors debate the formerly blind man's identity. These are different men and different degrees of agreement.

Both name Solomon's portico in the Temple setting. Acts gathers Peter, John, the healed man, and the astonished people there; John describes Jesus walking there at Dedication. The location comparison does not merge the occasions.

Both apostolic healing accounts redirect a crowd away from crediting the human messengers. Peter denies that personal power or godliness made the man walk; Paul and Barnabas reject the Lystra crowd's response and point to the living Creator. Their particular misconceptions differ.

Peter uses the ancestral God formula naming Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Exodus records God's self-identification to Moses with those patriarchs. Acts then speaks of Jesus' glorification; that further application is not a verbatim part of Exodus' bush statement.

Peter recalls handing over and denying Jesus before a Pilate who had decided on release. Luke narrates Pilate wanting release, the crowd's insistence, and his yielding to their demand. The speech and narrative correspond without adding another release attempt or shifting every agent into one undifferentiated group.

Acts recalls asking for a murderer instead of the Holy and Righteous One. Luke records the demand for Barabbas and explains his imprisonment for insurrection and murder. Acts supplies its own titles for Jesus rather than quoting those titles from these Luke verses.

Peter names Jesus the Author of life and testifies to God raising Him. John records Jesus' self-description as Resurrection and Life and His promise to believers. The related life-and-resurrection claims have different speakers and immediate settings.

Both connect restored health with faith related to Jesus. Mark explicitly names the woman's faith; Acts describes faith in Jesus' name and faith through Him without naming a particular human possessor of that faith. The patient, condition, and stated form of faith differ.

Both speak of ignorance surrounding Jesus' death. Peter names his hearers and their rulers; Luke records Jesus praying forgiveness for 'them' because they do not know what they do. The pronoun's referents are not automatically made coextensive with every person in Peter's address.

Both relate the Christ's suffering to the prophets' scriptural message. Luke has Jesus explain suffering and glory through Moses and the prophets; Peter says God fulfilled what He announced about suffering. These are related interpretations in different settings, not independent historical attestations.

Both use the wiping-away image for sins or lawlessness. Isaiah has God announce blotting out and not remembering; Peter calls for repentance and turning so sins may be wiped away. The command to the hearers is distinguished from God's described act.

Both anticipate the ascended Jesus' coming. Acts 1 records the messengers' return promise; Peter speaks of refreshing from the Lord and sending the appointed Christ. This develops a future expectation rather than dating its fulfillment.

Both describe God's speaking through His holy prophets from long ago. Luke places that formula with salvation in David's house; Acts places it with Christ's heavenly reception and restoration. The shared prophetic-history language does not equate the two complete announcements or settle every meaning of restoration.

Moses' promised prophet from the brothers, like Moses and to be heard, supplies the core citation. Acts also says to hear everything the prophet speaks. The prophet comparison is preserved without making Deuteronomy explicitly name Jesus.

Both warn against failing to hear the promised prophet's words. Deuteronomy says God will exact retribution from the unheeding person; Acts states destruction from among the people. The consequence is related but the entire English sentence is not presented as identical.

Samuel is established as the Lord's prophet and recipient of His word in the older narrative. Peter names Samuel at the beginning of his prophetic sequence. This supplies the named prophet's role, not a claim that these verses contain a particular oracle naming Pentecost or Jesus' resurrection.

Peter invokes the Abrahamic seed-and-blessing promise. Genesis speaks of all the earth's nations being blessed in Abraham's seed; Acts says all the families of the earth. The scope terms and Peter's covenant-heir application remain distinct.

Both describe a saving mission through turning away wickedness among God's people. Isaiah names the Deliverer, Zion, and Jacob; Acts names God's Servant sent first to its hearers to bless them through turning. This is a possible prophetic-background comparison with different titles and wording.

deferred.reason: Joseph Barsabbas/Justus and Matthias are named as the two candidates here; no other same-name person or the unnamed members of another disciple group is identified with either without evidence.
This particular list of peoples and regions is not equated with later church addressees or used to infer that named visitors founded churches in their homelands.

The continued regional and visitor list has no sufficiently close retained counterpart. Shared place-names alone are not used to identify later people or to assert an unrecorded founding of the Roman church.
The man's particular request for alms from Peter and John is not assigned to another beggar encounter or treated as a verbatim fulfillment of a general giving command.
The man's expectation of receiving something is retained as stated. It is not equated with the explicit faith-for-healing perception in the separate Lystra narrative.

review_notes: Stable Acts 1–3 peer preview only: 99 source units,94 supported sources,96 pairs,5 deferrals. All retained targets have been read with actual context. The final Acts1–5 proposal supersedes this preview; no completion credit is requested from the preview.
